title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
summary: Assign stable permissions to organizational roles and enforce those permissions at every agent tool and data boundary.
overview: Role-based access control maps users or service identities to roles and roles to permitted operations. In an agent architecture, it controls which tools can be invoked and which classes of resources can be accessed. The model can explain a requested action, but it cannot grant itself a role or establish the caller's identity.

Roles work best when they correspond to stable job responsibilities. Keep role assignment separate from role activation and apply separation of duties where one actor must not initiate and approve the same operation. Resource ownership, geography, and changing context may require additional attribute-based controls beyond a role alone.

production.poc: A prototype often uses one developer credential. Replace it with explicit reader and operator roles before exposing shared enterprise systems.
production.production: Production centralizes role definitions, validates identity tokens, and checks permissions at tool services rather than only hiding interface buttons. Record the acting user and service identity separately.
production.scale: At scale, role lifecycle and review matter as much as request-time enforcement. Prevent role explosion, revoke departed users promptly, and test nested-role behavior and privileged service-account scope.

components.name: Identity provider
components.role: Authenticates principals and issues trusted identity and group assertions.

components.name: Role directory
components.role: Maps approved organizational membership to stable role definitions.

components.name: Permission policy
components.role: Defines which actions and resource classes each role may access.

components.name: Enforcement point
components.role: Checks the actual tool or data request before execution.

components.name: Access review record
components.role: Tracks role grants, removals, exceptions, and separation-of-duties decisions.

flow.title: Authenticate principal
flow.description: Validate the session or delegated token and establish both user and workload identity.

flow.title: Resolve roles
flow.description: Load current approved roles without accepting role names from prompt content.

flow.title: Map permissions
flow.description: Determine whether the requested operation belongs to the active role's allowed capability set.

flow.title: Check constraints
flow.description: Apply separation of duties and any additional resource-specific conditions.

flow.title: Enforce at service
flow.description: Reject unauthorized operations even if the agent or interface attempted to invoke them.

flow.title: Audit outcome
flow.description: Record the action, principal, active role, policy version, and allow or deny result.

useCase.title: Separating invoice preparation from payment approval
useCase.situation: A shared-services center uses an assistant to retrieve invoices, explain exceptions, and prepare payment proposals.
useCase.problem: A broadly privileged integration account lets clerks accidentally request operations reserved for treasury approvers.
useCase.requirement: The assistant must support each employee's work while preserving existing responsibility boundaries.
useCase.architecture: Reader, preparer, and approver roles govern tool permissions, with an independent check preventing self-approval.
runtime: A clerk asks the agent to prepare a payment proposal; the gateway authorizes creation but rejects release of funds.
An authorized approver later reviews the proposal under a distinct identity and the payment service rechecks the role.
useCase.failure: If directory synchronization fails, privileged actions deny access rather than reusing an indefinitely stale grant.
useCase.impact: Track denied privileged requests, stale memberships, self-approval attempts, and time to revoke access. Role checks support the process but do not replace financial controls.

tradeoffs.benefit: Permissions align with understandable job responsibilities.
tradeoffs.cost: Fine-grained exceptions can create too many roles.

tradeoffs.benefit: Policy changes remain consistent across tools.
tradeoffs.cost: Directory availability and cache freshness become dependencies.
Complex hierarchies can grant unexpected effective authority.

failures.scenario: An agent service account has broader access than the user
failures.detection: Effective permissions exceed the delegated role.
failures.recovery: Intersect service capability with user authority before execution.

failures.scenario: A departed employee retains a cached role
failures.detection: Revocation tests or directory versions reveal stale membership.
failures.recovery: Expire cached grants and invalidate active privileged sessions.

mistakes.mistake: Authorizing only at the chat interface
mistakes.fix: Enforce permissions in every backing tool service.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting role claims from user text
Creating a role for each individual exception
mistakes.fix: Add scoped attributes or redesign responsibilities.

whenToUse: Job responsibilities map to stable permission bundles.
Multiple tools need consistent action-level controls.
Separation of duties is an explicit requirement.
whenNotToUse: Every access decision depends mainly on changing context.
Roles cannot express resource ownership or tenant boundaries.
A tiny public read-only service needs no differentiated access.

references.title: NIST SP 800-162: attribute based access control
